cassius-coolidge-1905-08-25.A1:
KILLS ONE NEGRO; DISABLES ANOTHER Cassius Coolidge Shoots Two Men of His Own Race and Is Sub- dued by Police—Five Patrol- men Chase Him.
The fusillade from the revolvers of four policemen, as they ran for four blocks in pursuit of Cassius Coolidge, a negro, who had shot Oscar and Harry Grimes, two other negroes, sent residents on O'Fallon street, Cass avenue and Ninth street scurrying to shelter shortly after 9 o'clock last evening.

Patrolman Patrick Somers, who led the chase, finally overtook Coolidge, and at the point of his revolver forced the big negro to surrender. The chase was shot in the abdomen and died at the City Hospital shortly before 9 o'clock. A bullet from Coolidge's revolver pierced the left groin of Harry Grimes, and his condition is said to be critical.

The shooting was the outcome of a fight the three negroes had Thursday. Coolidge went to the mouth of the alley on the north side of O'Fallon street between Tenth and Eleventh streets last evening and met the Grimes brothers. Without a word, he drew his revolver and began firing. When his victims had fallen to the ground, he started to run through the alley toward Cass avenue.

Patrolman Somers reached the scene in time to see Coolidge fleeing. He yelled at the negro, but the fugitive refused to halt. One shot was fired in the air, but Coolidge only captured his place. Then Somers shot to kill onward.

The chase continued to Cass avenue, where Coolidge turned and fled south on Tenth street. Patrolmen Dwyer, Ballard, Bene and Sergeant Meyers joined the pursuit. They turned Coolidge when he reached O'Fallon street, and he ran north to Cass avenue, through the alley that parallels Eleventh street. When overtaken and forced to yield his weapon, Coolidge regretted his action and attacked Sergeant Meyers. He was clubbed into submission.

Oscar Grimes, the negro who was killed, was a porter and lives at No. 1333 North Tenth street. Harry Grimes is 17 years old and lives at No. 1911 North Tenth street.

Coolidge is also a porter and lives at No. 1333 North Tenth street.

george-davis-bogue-chitto.A1:
TWO LINCOLN WHITECAPPERS.
Charged with Interfering with a Negro Mail Carrier.
United States Marshals W. O. Ligon and Edgar S. Wilson, Jr., came in this morning, or rather last night from Bogue Chitto, having in custody Douglass Holloway and John Ratliff, two white men who stand charged with interfering with and bulldozing George Davis, a negro mail carrier between Bogue Chitto and Ambler. They are alleged to have fired into the mail carrier's house and threatened to kill him if he did not quit carrying the mail over that route.

Four men were indicted by the Federal grand jury for this same offense, but only two of them have been arrested so far.

Holloway and Ratliff were arraigned before Commissioner Moseley this morning, waived examination and were placed under bond in the sum of $1,000 each to secure their attendance on the next session of Federal Court in this city.—Clarion-Ledger.

From Money He Didn't Have.

Roland Jones, a big black negro, was the direct cause of a lot of excitement Monday night, and yesterday morning Justice Crutchfield separated Roland from $10 that he didn't have. The specific offense with which Roland was charged, was that of beating one Laura Brackett against the peace and dignity of the Commonwealth and Laura's head. But an officer fired at Roland to make him stop, and the report became current that some one had been killed. There was confusion for a while.

Simon Forsythe assisted materially in the circumstances that went to make up the report of a man's death. Shortly after the pistol was fired and the Roland herein before mentioned, started to run, Mr. Forsythe was found in a condition that defied all the powers of the officers and others to shake. He had tanked himself and gone off to a secluded street, and there fallen into the arms of Morpheus.

Forsythe received twenty days in which to sleep it off.

Robert Parker and Gertrude Fitzgerald had lots of trouble last night, and the magistrates worked overtime fixing up the warrants. It was all threshed out before Justice John, and the two negroes ordered to get out and stay out. They got.

Thomas J. Wood was fined $10 for trespassing upon the premises of Mr. James E. Woodfin.

Joe Vaughan didn't like the countenance of William Woolfolk, and, therefore, tried to change it. He didn't have the five that was asked of him.

Eugene Hewmert, for being a vagrant, got thirty days in jail.

The Justice folded up the book, looked ever at the pen and went out and voted, after telling the judges what he thought about this primary and the one previous.

sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A2:
SANK MAJORS ON TRIAL FOR CRIMINAL ASSAULT Special to The Light.
Waco, Tex., Aug. 2.—Sank Majors was brought into the court room of the Nineteenth district court this morning on trial for his life, the charge being that of criminally assaulting Mrs. B. Robert of Golinda on July 11, also beating and stabbing his victim until she was left lying unconscious, the husband of one month coming home to find her lying on the gallery of their little home bruised, bleeding and apparently lifeless.

Majors and Robert had had some words about crossing a piece of land, and were not on good terms, and it was thought by many at first that Majors merely attacked Mrs. Robert cut of anger and that nothing further had been attempted, but the grand jury, after investigating the matter and having Mrs. Robert before them returned an indictment for criminal assault, thus putting Majors on trial for his life. Prior to agreeing to try the negro here a promise was secured from the people of Golinda that they would allow the law to take its course, as they were greatly incensed at first and in fact are yet. Mobs followed every possible trail which might lead to Majors for nearly two weeks, and until he was captured at Lockhart, Majors was brought to Waco from Austin when the grand jury met, and has been under guard since.

When indicted by the grand jury last Friday Judge Surratt at once set the case down for Wednesday, August 2, in order that swift justice might be given the negro in case of guilt or innocence being established. A special venire was summoned by the officers and everything made ready. Governor Lanham offered a reward of $300 for Majors and Sheriffs Sanders and Jackman received this.
sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A5:
NEGRO LYNCHED AT WACO.
A Texas Mob Hanged Confessed Criminal at Early Hour.
final at Early Hour.

WACO, Tex., August 8.—At 2 o'clock this morning mounted citizens numbering about 000 surrounded the court house and jail, and after making prisoners of Sheriff Tilley, the jailer and all the deputy sheriffs, broke open the jail, took Sank Majors, colored, out, and after hearing his confession hanged him from the new bridge.

Majors had recently been convicted of criminal assault and given the death penalty, but had been granted a new trial by Judge Surratt, in order that there might be no opportunity for the court of criminal appeals to revise the sentence on a technicality.
sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A7:
ALL IS NOW QUIET.
Special to The Light.

Waco, Tex., Aug. 8.—Sank Majors, the negro, convicted of criminal assault upon Mrs. B. Robert near Golinda on July 11, was taken from the county jail at 2 o'clock this morning by an armed mob of three hundred people and swung to a beam across the new bridge across the Erazos river. The presence of the mob was in entire surprise to the officers and they had the jail completely surrounded before the officers were aware of their presence.

The mob made a demand for the keys of the jail, which were refused. The leaders then, armed with sledge hammers, began to batter the doors down. It took half an hour to get the outside door down and during this time Sheriff Tilley remonstrated with the men in every possible manner. They told the sheriff they did not want to hurt anybody, but had come for Sank Majors and intended to get him.

After getting the front door open the inner doors were an easy prey. The negro was reached and then seized. He was taken down the main street to the square and a halt was made there with the avowed intention of burning him. The husband of the outraged woman is said to have made the request on behalf of his wife that the negro be hanged, and this was done.

The negro was left hanging on the bridge for an hour and the men who did the work rode quietly out of the city. They are supposed to be the friends and neighbors of the woman, who was the victim of the atrocious deed.

Majors had been tried and convicted and given the death penalty. A new trial was secured on a technicality and the same was set for Wednesday of this week. Tiring of delays in the court and possible further delays, are the reasons assigned for the lynching of Majors.

Everything was quiet this morning and the lynching is the topic for conversation on the streets.
sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A9:
A Brutal Assault Upon a Defenseless Woman Avenged by a Mob of Neighbors After a New Trial Had Been Granted the Defendant.
OFFICERS WERE POWERLESS TO RESIST
Battering Rams Were Used Until a Total of Five Doors Were Smashed in by the Mob.—When Majors' Cell Was Reached He Was Taken Out and Hanged to the Brazos Bridge.
Waco. August 8.—Sanks Majors, the negro who on July 11 made a criminal assault on Mrs. B. Roberts, who lives near Golindo, fifteen miles from this place, was taken by a mob of approximately 2,000 people from the county jail here this morning between 1 and 2 o'clock and hanged. Majors was hanged on the new Brazos river bridge on Washington street.

The mob came from the Golindo section as far as can be learned.

It formed at the jail at 11:45 o'clock. Everything worked as if moved by clock work.

It was first the intention of the mob to burn Majors on the public square. It was dissuaded from this, however.

The mob first broke down the outer gate to the jail. Then one by one they wielded battering rails until a total of five doors were smashed in to get to Majors.

The negro heard the knocks against the doors of steel and retained a stoical attitude as the mob hammered its way toward him.

At last the cell in which Majors was confined was reached. Majors was jerked from this cell and vigorously hustled ahead of the ringleaders.

Mayor Jim Baker and Sheriff George Tilley were overpowered. The mob was too strong to be combatted. It came for Majors' life, and it came prepared to take that life, even though it cost bloodshed.

The leaders of the mob preserved perfect discipline. After Majors was hanged to the bridge—he was swung from the center bent—the mob dispersed. In twenty minutes the city assumed its usual midnight stillness.
sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A15:
ARGUED FOR HOUR WHETHER TO BURN OR HANG THE NEGRO Fifteen Hundred Texans Battered Down Jail Doors at Waco, Seized Prisoner Under Death Sentence to Whom New Trial Had Been Granted, and After Long Parley as to Method of Lynching to Be Adopted Finally Decided on the More Merciful Course. VICTIM SHOWED LITTLE INTEREST IN THE PROCEEDINGS.
Houston, Tex., Aug. 8—At 2 this morning 500 mounted men rode into the city of Waco, and were joined by 1,000 on foot. They made their way to the county jail, and there used improvised battering rams and sledge hammers to break their way through the steel doors and to the cell occupied by Sank Majors, a negro.

Majors was bound and taken to the jail yard, where a conference was held for nearly an hour regarding the fate that should be met on time. The mounted lynchers had bought with them oil, it being their plan to burn him at the stake. In the conference many speeches were made, some advocating fire and others the rope. A vote was at length taken, and the arguments for the more merciful course finally prevailed. The rope route was chosen by a small majority.

Majors maintained a cool demeanor during the ordeal. He displayed a stolid indifference except when the question of burning him was up. He asked to be either shot or hanged, saying he did not like fire.

He was quickly taken to the railroad bridge, a few blocks from the jail, where one end of a rope was noosed about his neck and the other fastened to the bridge.

sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A20:
NEGRO FLOGGED FOR DENOUNCING LYNCHING
Special to The Light.

Waco, Tex., Aug. 10.—A negro, named Jim Lawyer, was taken from his neighbor's home near Bruceville, this county, last night, and given a sound flogging.

This was occasioned by some statements that were made by him in condemning the whites for lynching Sank Majors. There were about twenty men who called upon Lawyer, and after hearing his statement they reported him and told him that it would be better for him to hunt other climes.

He took them at their word and left this morning.

There is still considerable feeling with reference to the lynching, and further talk by the negroes will be to their own trouble.

SATURDAY, AUGUST 12, 1905.
TRIFLING WITH JUSTICE.
The Albany (Ga.) Herald declares that "the Texans have reached the point where they will stand hitched for an orderly trial, but they kick promptly out of the traces when dilatory tactics are resorted to."

This remark was brought out in commenting on a recent occurrence at Waco. A negro had committed the crime which no true Southern man can or will forgive. On the assurance that he should rave a speedy trial, the people refrained from interfering with him. He was tried, found guilty, convicted and sentenced. Then his lawyer convicted and sentenced. Then his lawyer on some pretense or other moved for a new trial which he was granted. A few nights later he was taken from the jail by an armed crowd and hung after having confessed his guilt.

It will be said that the act of the mob, if it must be so designated, was a trifling with justice. Perhaps it was, but the first trifling with justice was in the courthouse when the judge granted the brute a new trial. As we understand the testimony, there was no
It is a mistake and a wrong for a Southern court to allow dilatory tactics in a case of this kind. The people of the South will not stand for it. As The Herald says: "The average community in the South will, except in cases somewhat rare, remain quiet if negroes accused of the unnamable crime are given immediate trial, but as surely as technicalities of the law are appealed to or other means taken to induce delay in the application of justice, public indignation breaks loose and sweeps everything before it, just as it did in Waco night before last."

We insist that a court has no moral right to thus trifle with justice. If the negro had not had a fair trial, or if there had been doubt of his guilt, it would have been just and right to give him a new trial, but we do not learn that his trial was not fair, or that there was any doubt in his case. Justice was trifled with and the people refused to stand for it. That is all there is about it.
sank-majors-waco-1905-08-08.A23:
HOW MAJOR'S LYNCHING IS REGARDED IN WACO.
Special to The Light.

Waco, Tex., Aug. 12.—There has been little said by the white people since the lynching of Sank Majors, though the negroes have been saying a good deal. The white people are not going to stand for any great amount of talk of this kind, and those negroes who have been the loudest have already seen their folly.

The white people say as long as the negroes keep their tongues and places they will not disturb them, but if there is any talking of a nature that is tended to stir up any further feeling there may be trouble.

The announcement made by Governor Lanham that he proposed to investigate the lynching of Majors, was read with interest, but little commen was made about it. It is stated that he will have no trouble in getting such information as he may desire.

Letters to the Editor
Letters to the Editor.
I have been a constant, if not a close, newspaper reader and a liberal patron of the press for a number of years, and I feel safe in saying that these agencies have much to do with moulding public sentiment and influencing human character and conduct. This being true, all newspapers, especially our leading dailies, it occurs to me, ought to be exceedingly careful and guarded in the use of their editorial space. Heretofore The Advertiser has been conservative and sound on almost all questions affecting public interest and safety, and has been, and is now, regarded as a criterion by not a few. For this reason, I feel compelled to take issue with the editorial in your issue of the 12th inst., under the caption, "Trifling With Justice," as it most certainly tends towards the encouragement of the mob spirit, if it is not an endorsement of mob law, from the disastrous and woeful consequences of which may "angels and ministers of grace defend us."

Now, I want it understood in advance that I am not here trying in anyway to defend the criminal, the subject of this editorial, but my purpose is simply to use what power and influence I may have to check and discourage the mob spirit and to uphold the majesty of the law which has too often in recent years been wantonly and ruthlessly set aside and trampled in the mire of hate and revenge, thereby lowering the standard of civilization and Christianity in our beautiful Southland. The editorial to which I have reference is to follow.
"Trifling With Justice.

"The Albany (Ga.) Herald declares that 'the Texans have reached the point where they will stand hitched for an orderly trial, but they kick promptly out of the traces when dilatory tactics are resorted to."

"This remark was brought out in commenting on a recent occurrence at Waco. A negro had committed the crime which no true Southern man can or will forgive. On the assurance that he should have a speedy trial, the people refrained from interfering with him. He was tried, found guilty, convicted and sentenced. Then his lawyer on some pretense or other moved for a new trial which was granted. A few nights later he was taken from the jail by an armed crowd and hung after having confessed his guilt.

"It will be said that the act of the mob, if it must be so designated, was a trifling with justice. Perhaps it was, but the first trifling with justice was in the courthouse when the judge granted the brute a new trial. As we understand the testimony, there was no doubt of his guilt, even leaving out his own confession. He had a fair trial, his guilt was established and he was fairly convicted. That should have ended it, and his execution should have followed in due time. Then there would have been no occasion for a lynching and none would have occurred. Justice would have been satisfied and the good town of Waco would not have been heralded to the world as the scene of mob law."

Now, if this editorial, when considered as a whole, does not give countenance and encouragement to mob law, then I fail to understand it, and the fact that it comes from the editorial page of one of the largest and most influential dallies in the State may be taken to some extent as an explanation as to why the Governor is so often called upon to order out the military to protect some wretch, already in the custody of the law, from the fury and rage of a lawless mob. And, I might add, prevent good men from committing deeds of violence under great provocation and heat of passion which they must ever after regret. The mob spirit will get in enough of its bloody work in spite of all the conservative influences we can bring to bear upon it. So let us all beware.

In this case The Advertiser has been hasty, if not rash, in jumping at conclusions and in its condemnation of this Texas court as the following excerpt from this editorial will show: "It will be said that the act of the mob, if it must be so designated, was a trifling with justice. Perhaps it was, but the first trifling with justice was in the courthouse where the judge granted the brute a new trial." Here you not only assume as facts circumstances about which you confess you have no personal knowledge, but you prefer a serious indictment against this trial judge, with nothing but naked conclusions to sustain it: "The first trifling with justice," you say, "was in the courthouse." This means, of course, that the judge who sat upon the trial of this case was moved by some corrupt motive in granting the new trial which you style "trifling with justice." I haven't the slightest information as to who the judge was that presided in this trial, but from a general knowledge of courts and judges, I would be willing to stake my reputation as a lawyer on the assertion that this judge had sound legal grounds for granting this new trial, and that he did it reluctantly. Perhaps there was some defect in the indictment, illegality in the organization of the grand jury that found the bill or some other irregularity that was called to the court's attention in this motion for the new trial which would not support a conviction and sentence, and on which he knew he would be reversed if an appeal was taken. In other words, he was clearly convinced that the defendant had not been tried and convicted according to law. If that was true, no higher duty could rest on the trial judge than to grant this new trial, and he would have violated his duty to himself, to this country and to his God to have refused it. But The Advertiser assumes that such was not the case and jumps at the conclusion that the defendant "had a fair trial, his guilt was established and he was fairly convicted," but if put through a cross-examination no doubt it would admit that it was "talking through its hat" and that it really knew nothing about the real facts in the case. Such reckless and unwarranted attacks upon the courts has a tendency to destroy confidence in the efficiency and integrity of our judicial tribunals and furnishes all the excuses the lawless and vicious need for breaking down jail doors, overpowering sheriffs and other legally constituted authorities and staining their hands with the blood of a fellow being already in the custody of the law. Let it be understood once for all, that every person who participates in a lynching is not only guilty of murder under the laws of this State, but God will hold each responsible as a particeps criminis.

As stated above, newspapers wield great influence in moulding public opinion and sentiment and a great daily like The Advertiser ought to be more guarded in its expressions on such momentous questions. Such editorials coming from such a source are, to say the least of it, misleading and tends to encourage the mob spirit. It seems to me that the press of the country is getting entirely too loose in such matters. In support of this assertion, I will mention a most deplorable tragedy that took place down in Coffee County some months ago. A young woman took umbrage at some statement reflecting on her character alleged to have been made by her brother-in-law, at which she worked herself into a great heat of passion and, provided with the deadly revolver, she started "on the warpath," and as soon as she came up with him she whipped it out and, without one word of warning, she shot him to death. And, if I remember correctly, The Montgomery Journal, in commenting on the bloody deed, not only tried to justify the act, but actually applauded the poor, misguided young woman in the commission of the horrible crime. LYNCHING PLANS FAIL
HAVERSTRAW MOB OUT.
Companion of Negro Who Killed Policeman Threatened.
Haverstraw, N. Y., Aug. 20 (Special).—A threatened riot, growing out of the shooting of two policemen of this place by a negro, has created tremendous excitement here all day and tonight. One policeman was killed by the negro and the other policeman is expected to die from his wounds. The negro murderer escaped and is still at large, but another negro who was with him at the time of the shooting was caught in Cornwall and brought here to-day, and he came near being lynched by a large crowd of angry citizens. He was taken to the jail at New City for safekeeping, and to-night another crowd went there with the avowed intention of lynching him, but failed to get at him.

The shooting took place last night near the brickyards. Several negroes employed there as laborers have been getting drunk after they received their pay Saturday nights and engaging in bloody shooting affrays. Patrolmen Cahill, Springstead and Call started out last night to disarm drunken negroes at the brickyards, and on the road to the yards they met two negroes, halted them and asked them if they carried revolvers. One of the negroes, known as "Steamboat" Brown, declared that no white man could take away his gun. He drew his revolver and shot Cahill dead, sending a bullet through his heart. Then he shot Springstead in the stomach. Springstead fell fainting on the road. Call ran away. He said later that he went to get help for his wounded associates.

"Steamboat" Brown and the other negro escaped, but as soon as the information of the shooting spread through Haverstraw several hundred white men armed themselves and began a search. It was believed that the two negroes had left town, and messages were sent to neighboring towns to arrest the fugitives.

While a large posse searched the woods and hills near Haverstraw, to-day, Constable Tow-
h a large posse searched the woods and
hills near Haverstraw to-day. Constable Towers,
of Garnersville, went to Newburg on information that "Steamboat" Brown had relatives at Fishkill. With the assistance of the Newburg police he arrested a colored man named Sisco, who had been seen to jump off a train at Cornwall, believed to be the negro who was with Brown at the time of the shooting. Sisco told contradictory stories. He was taken to Haverstraw to-day with the expectation that he could be identified by Call.

His arrival here became known quickly, and a crowd of several hundred men gathered, threatening to lynch the negro. District Attorney Lee, of Rockland County, made a speech to the angry crowd, saying that the law would punish the murderer of Policeman Cahill and that any mob. He urged the crowd to get the negro, however, and returned.

Fearing violence to the prisoner, however, the police took Sisco to New City, where he was lodged in jail. To-night, when the disposition of the prisoner became known, another large crowd gathered, and over two hundred men went to New City, declaring that they would take the prisoner out of the jail and hang him. They failed to get the negro, however, and returned.

The supervisors of Rockland County have offered a reward of $1,000 for the capture of Cahill's murderer, and citizens of Haverstraw have offered an additional reward of $1,000. It is said to-night that Policeman Springstead probably cannot live. Both Cahill and Springstead have been popular policemen here. They are credited with many good arrests, and it was said to-day that they were the only men who had the courage to make arrests in the brickyards when there was trouble among the laborers there.

MacDonald, the British Minister, and other officials; the Foreign Office adheres to secrecy; popular opinion inclines to belief in the continuance of the war. — Lord Curzon of Kedleston resigned as Viceroy of India, owing to differences arising from the new scheme of army administration; the Earl of Minto has been appointed his successor. — German views of the Russian assembly show great divergence; the Socialist papers call the manifesto an imperial joke.

DOMESTIC.—The President was pleased with the results of his conference with Baron Rosen and the peace outlook is regarded at Oyster Bay as hopeful; in Portsmouth, among the Russian delegation, pessimism prevails, according to unofficial information received by them from St. Petersburg, the Council of State has decided that no further concessions shall be made to Japanese demands; the Japanese preserve their air of cheerful belief in peace resulting from the conference. — A dispatch from Cleveland said that Walter F. Minor, the telegrapher on duty at Mentor when the Twentleth Century Limited was wrecked, would probably be arrested. — There were forty-five new cases and four deaths from yellow fever in New-Orleans. — Cardinal Gibbons, at Baltimore, issued a statement declaring that the decision in the Rospigliosi case was based on unimpeachable records, and that the case would not be reopened. — Over five hundred persons attending the laying of a cornerstone of a Pittsburg synagogue were thrown fifteen feet into a cellar by the collapse of a platform.

CITY.—Two Chinamen were probably fatally wounded in a tong fight at No. 18 Pell-st. — Two policemen were shot and one was killed by a negro in Haverstraw; the murderer escaped, but a companion who was caught was lodged in New-City jail after a large crowd threatened to lynch him. — The steamer Sagamii, from the Far East, reported that three Chinese firemen believing the vessel unlucky, had jumped over board. It was reported here that Venezuela was buying arms and ammunition in preparation for war. A patrolman was badly beaten by ruffians in Newtown. Pushcart pedlers, irritated over business, threaten a general strike against everybody in general. Meetings of the city and county Republican committees will be held this week. The police of Williamsburg arrested an Italian accused of having written blackmailing letters.

Negro Shoots Two Policemen.
Haverstraw, N. Y., Aug. 21.—One policeman is dead and another is not expected to live, as the result of an attempt to disperse a crowd of negroes in the vicinity of the brick yards. The negroes had been drinking and Policemen Cahill, Springstead and Call went to the place to quell the disorder. On the outskirts of the crowd they met a negro named Brown, who, declaring that no one should take away his pistol, pulled the weapon and began firing. Cahill was instantly killed and Springstead so badly wounded he is not expected to live. Brown escaped.

NEGRO SHOOTS TO KILL.
Haverstraw, N. Y., Aug. 22—One policeman is dead and another is not expected to live as the result of an attempt last night to disperse a crowd of negroes in the vicinity of the brickyard. A negro named Brown is said to have done the shooting. He is still at large. A companion named Sisco was captured today. The negroes had been drinking and Policemen Cahill, Springstead and Call went to the place to quell the disturbance. On the outskirts of the crowd they met Brown who, declaring that no one should take away his pistol, pulled the weapon and began firing. Cahill was instantly killed and Springstead so badly wounded he is not expected to live.
sisco-haverstraw-1905-08-20.A9:
HELD FOR HAVERSTRAW MURDER.
Negro Waiter Arrested, Charged With Killing Policeman.
Police of the West 47th-st. station arrested last night Jesse Crisfield, a negro waiter, charged with the murder of John Cahill, a policeman, in Haverstraw, last Saturday. Crisfield said he lives at No. 324 West 59th-st. The police say he was arrested on information given them by Timothy P. Collins, of No. 113 West 14th-st. They say that in his possession among his baggage they found a loaded revolver.
sisco-haverstraw-1905-08-20.A11:
NEGROES UNRESTRAINED.
Not Safe to Walk in Haverstraw Streets After Dark—Laborer Robbed.
[By Telegraph to The Tribune.] strawy N. Y. Aug 29. Such lit

have the six special policemen sworn in here had on the lawless negro element that last night a big negro held up a pedestrian and robbed him of everything he had about him except his underwear. The man, a laborer, was passing through a dark street, when suddenly a negro shoved a revolver in his face and demanded his money.

The man said he had only a few cents in change. "Then," said the negro, "I'll take your clothes." "You can have anything I have, only don't shoot," replied the laborer and in a trice he was stripped of most of his clothing.

The victim made a dash for the nearest house, an eighth of a mile away, where he was provided with a suit of clothes and went home.

The reports that Father McGuire and Father O'Reilly have appealed to the New-York police for protection are untrue. The priests say that they desire only protection for the people of Haverstraw and will make every effort to get the licenses of the saloons which the negroes patronize revoked.

There are about 2,000 negroes employed in the brick yards here and they have terrorized the whole town. It is not safe to stir out after dark. Holdups and insults are an everyday occurrence, although the six/special patrolmen have improved matters somewhat.

Every Saturday night many negro women come up from New-York and join with the townspeople to make Saturday night and Sunday periods of wild carousal and disorder.
